### Comparing Grout Options for Ceramic Floors

| Grout Type | Cost | Durability | Mold Resistance | Ease of Maintenance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Sanded Cementitious** 🏗️ | Low | Good | Moderate | Requires sealing; porous |
| **Unsanded Cementitious** 🏗️ | Low | Moderate | Low | Requires sealing; prone to cracking in floor expansion |
| **Epoxy** 🧪 | High | Excellent | High | Non-porous; very difficult to install |
| **Urethane** 🎨 | Medium | High | High | Flexible; easier to install than epoxy |

#### 1. Cementitious Grout (Sanded)
This is the most common choice for floors because the sand adds strength. However, standard cement grout is porous. In a steamy bathroom, if not sealed perfectly, it will eventually absorb moisture and harbor mold spores. You would need to reseal it every 1–3 years.

#### 2. Epoxy Grout
This is a two-part mixture of epoxy resin and filler. It is virtually non-porous, meaning water and mold have nowhere to hide. It’s incredibly durable and dishwasher-safe, which makes it excellent for bathrooms. The downside is that it’s significantly more expensive and tricky to work with—it skins over quickly and is hard to clean off the tile once it sets.

#### 3. Urethane Grout
A newer, more affordable middle ground. It’s more flexible than cement and much more chemical-resistant. It’s pre-mixed (no ratio to worry about) and offers better stain resistance than standard grout, though it still isn't as chemically inert as pure epoxy.

### Recommendation for Your Budget
Since you're avoiding expensive options like marble, **Sanded Cementitious Grout** is likely your most cost-effective floor. However, to keep that mold at bay, you should use a quality, mold-inhibiting sealer and keep the room ventilated.
